opus-5.5.text:
Booking a flight is a pretty narrow, well-specified task. The goal is clear, the interface is familiar, there's a ton of training data that looks like it, and the whole thing takes a few minutes and maybe a dozen actions. If you get it mostly right, you're done. So when a model can do that, it's a real milestone, but it's showing competence in the easiest corner of the space.

What people actually mean by full agentic computer use is much broader. It's the kind of thing a remote worker does over a day or a week. You're juggling many applications, often obscure or internal ones you've never seen. You're working under goals that are vague and change as you go. You have to notice when something has gone wrong, figure out why, and recover, instead of confidently continuing down a broken path. You have to hold context across hundreds or thousands of steps and keep track of what you've already tried. Small error rates per step compound badly over long horizons. Being 95% reliable on each action is fine for a ten-step task and disastrous for a thousand-step one.

There's also the question of judgment. When do you ask for clarification? When do you stop because something seems off, like a charge that looks wrong or an email that shouldn't go out? A lot of real work is less about clicking the right buttons and more about knowing what the right thing to do is when the instructions don't cover it.

So I think of flight booking as roughly analogous to early benchmark wins in other domains. It tells you the basic capability is there, perception, clicking, filling forms, but the hard parts are long-horizon coherence, reliability, error recovery, and operating in unfamiliar, messy environments. Those are things we have much less training data for, and they're harder to get feedback on, because you often don't find out you messed up until much later. I'd expect a substantial gap, probably years rather than months, between "can book a flight" and "can do the computer-based parts of most jobs end to end."

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes basic actions such as clicking and filling forms from the challenge of maintaining coherence across hundreds or thousands of steps in a larger task.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the key thing is that booking a flight is a short-horizon task. It's a few dozen steps, the interface is fairly standardized, there's a clear success condition, and if you get it wrong the cost is low. You can imagine training a system on a huge number of these fairly stereotyped interactions and having it work. But that's very different from what we actually mean when we talk about agentic computer use, which is being able to do the kind of work a human employee does over a day, a week, a month.

The thing that distinguishes real agentic work is the long horizon and the lack of structure. You have to hold a lot of context in your head about what the goal actually is, decompose it into subtasks, deal with things going wrong, notice when an approach isn't working and back out of it, and recover from errors that compound over time. Booking a flight doesn't really test any of that. If you make a mistake on step three, you don't end up in some weird state forty steps later where you have to figure out what went wrong.

There's also the issue that short tasks are much easier to evaluate, which means they're much easier to optimize for. So you can get very good performance on the benchmarks that measure these things while the actual capability we care about, reliably doing messy, open-ended work for hours or days without a human stepping in, is still quite far off. The data on task horizons suggests this is improving, maybe doubling every several months, but when you look at where we are, the systems are still fairly reliable at tasks that take a human minutes, and reliability falls off quite steeply as you go to tasks that take hours. So I'd say the flight booking demos are evidence that the pieces exist, but not that the hard part has been solved.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts isolated, stereotyped steps in flight booking with coordinating actions over long, open-ended work, including decomposing goals and recovering from compounding errors.

astra-6.text:
Because booking a flight is a fairly short, well-specified task. You’re given a destination and dates, and there’s a clear point at which you’ve succeeded. A system could do that reliably and still struggle with work that requires sustained planning, dealing with unexpected problems, and figuring out what to do next without someone directing it.

Imagine asking it to run a research project. It has to break down an ambiguous objective, choose which questions to investigate, keep track of what it’s learned, and revise its approach when something doesn’t work. Being able to execute individual steps through a computer is necessary, but it doesn’t establish that the system can coordinate those steps over a long period.

So I’d distinguish between demonstrating a useful computer-use capability and demonstrating reliable, general agency. Booking a flight is evidence for the former, but by itself it tells you relatively little about the latter.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes executing individual computer steps from coordinating them over time, describing planning and adapting across a larger task as the additional challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, booking a flight is a fairly narrow, well-specified task. You know what success looks like, and you can often get there through a relatively short sequence of actions. That’s evidence of some ability to use a computer, but it doesn’t tell you whether a system can reliably carry out a much longer, less structured project.

The harder question is whether you can give it a goal that takes a person days or weeks, and have it figure out the steps, keep track of what it’s doing, notice when something goes wrong, and recover without someone constantly steering it. Small errors compound over long sequences of actions. So there’s a big gap between demonstrating a successful booking and being able to delegate substantial work to a system.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a short booking sequence with longer projects requiring the system to plan, track, and recover across many actions, conveying the challenge of coordinating simple actions into sustained behavior.
